Here's the link to my formalization of sequent natural deduction for constructive propositional logic: https://paste.sr.ht/~chabulhwi/4b940f96f570b793351db60f9b1fbca445a2eaa9.

I defined well-formed formulas in propositional logic as follows:

/-- Well-formed formulas in propositional logic. -/
inductive Wff : Type where
  | Tru : Wff
  | Fal : Wff
  | And (φ ψ : Wff) : Wff
  | Or  (φ ψ : Wff) : Wff
  | Imp (φ ψ : Wff) : Wff

The Wff.toProp function defined below translates a well-formed formula into a proposition in Lean's type theory.

namespace Wff

def toProp : Wff → Prop
  | Tru => True
  | Fal => False
  | And φ ψ => φ.toProp ∧ ψ.toProp
  | Or  φ ψ => φ.toProp ∨ ψ.toProp
  | Imp φ ψ => φ.toProp → ψ.toProp

end Wff

The sequent φ ⊢ ψ means that ψ is derivable from φ, and the notation ⊢ φ is an abbreviation for ⊤ ⊢ φ. My deduction system for propositional logic has the following inference rules:

  • id : φ ⊢ φ. The identity rule.
  • simpl : (⊢ φ) → (ψ ⊢ φ). The simplification rule.
  • syl : (φ ⊢ ψ) → (ψ ⊢ χ) → (φ ⊢ χ). The syllogism rule.
  • falE : ⊥ ⊢ φ. The elimination rule for falsity.
  • andI : (φ ⊢ ψ) → (φ ⊢ χ) → (φ ⊢ ψ ∧ χ). The introduction rule for conjunction.
  • andEL : ψ ∧ χ ⊢ ψ. The left elimination rule for conjunction.
  • andER : ψ ∧ χ ⊢ χ. The right elimination rule for conjunction.
  • orIL : φ ⊢ φ ∨ ψ. The left introduction rule for disjunction.
  • orIR : ψ ⊢ φ ∨ ψ. The right introduction rule for disjunction.
  • orE : (φ ⊢ ψ ∨ χ) → (φ ∧ ψ ⊢ θ) → (φ ∧ χ ⊢ θ) → (φ ⊢ θ). The elimination rule for disjunction.
  • impI : (φ ∧ ψ ⊢ χ) → (φ ⊢ ψ → χ). The introduction rule for implication.
  • impE : (φ ⊢ ψ → χ) → (φ ⊢ ψ) → (φ ⊢ χ). The elimination rule for implication.

I've successfully proven that every proposition translated from a sequent that has a derivation is true in Lean's type theory. Here's my proof:

namespace Sequent

/-- For all well-formed formulas `φ` and `ψ`, if `ψ` is derivable from `φ`, then the proposition
`φ.toProp → ψ.toProp` is true. -/
theorem toProp {φ ψ : Wff} (d : φ ⊢ ψ) (h : φ.toProp) : ψ.toProp :=
  match d with
  | id => h
  | simpl d => d.toProp trivial
  | @syl φ _χ ψ d₁ d₂ => d₂.toProp (d₁.toProp h)
  | falE => h.elim
  | @andI φ χ θ d₁ d₂ => ⟨d₁.toProp h, d₂.toProp h⟩
  | @andEL χ θ => h.1
  | @andER χ θ => h.2
  | @orIL  χ θ => Or.inl h
  | @orIR  χ θ => Or.inr h
  | @orE φ _χ _θ ψ or left right =>
      (or.toProp h).elim (and_imp.mp left.toProp h) (and_imp.mp right.toProp h)
  | @impI χ θ ψ d => and_imp.mp d.toProp h
  | @impE φ _χ ψ d₁ d₂ => (d₁.toProp h) (d₂.toProp h)

end Sequent

How can I translate a constructive proof of a propositional formula in Lean's type theory into a derivation of a sequent in my deduction system? I couldn't properly define the notion of a constructive proof of a propositional formula in Lean's type theory in the first place. Can anyone help me?

Just to clarify, do you mean this is what you want to prove?

example {φ ψ : Wff} (h : φ.toProp → ψ.toProp) : φ ⊢ ψ := sorry

possibly forbidding h to use Lean's axioms?

I guess so? The proof h should be constructed only from function abstraction, function application, certain constructors like And.intro, certain projections like And.left, and certain eliminators like Or.elim.

And do you intend to use metaprogramming? I don't think you'll be able to read the contents of h otherwise.
If you're trying to prove your system is equivalent to another (e.g. Hilbert), it might be better to define that other system using inductives rather than trying to mess with Lean's own system.
I plan to learn how to use metaprogramming in Lean, but I also want to know whether I can find a way to define the notion of a constructive proof of a propositional formula in Lean's type theory.
It sounds like you're asking for #print axioms, i.e. to verify that a proof doesn't use choice/propext/quot
I guess you're right. I don't want to use these axioms in this case, since I'm trying to ensure that my deduction system for constructive propositional logic can prove what it should prove.

I don't know much in this area, but I believe "proving things about proofs" means you have to use metaprogramming. That's the "meta" part (ditto for any other fancy proof manipulations). So you can read the meta code of #print axioms to see how to check for axioms. I don't think this is productive though.

inductive ProofType : Type → Type 1 where
  | unit  : ProofType Unit
  | empty : ProofType Empty
  | prod  {α β : Type} : ProofType α → ProofType β → ProofType (α × β)
  | sum   {α β : Type} : ProofType α → ProofType β → ProofType (α ⊕ β)
  | arrow {α β : Type} : ProofType α → ProofType β → ProofType (α → β)

namespace ProofType

infixr:35 " × " => prod
infixr:30 " ⊕ " => sum
infixr:25 " → " => arrow

def toProp {α : Type} : ProofType α → Prop
  | unit  => True
  | empty => False
  | @prod β γ t₁ t₂ => t₁.toProp ∧ t₂.toProp
  | @sum  β γ t₁ t₂ => t₁.toProp ∨ t₂.toProp
  | @arrow β γ t₁ t₂ => t₁.toProp → t₂.toProp

section

open ProofType

inductive HasTerm : {α : Type} → ProofType α → α → Type 1 where
  | fun_id {α : Type} {t : ProofType α} : HasTerm (t → t) id
  | fun_const {α β : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} {b : β} : HasTerm t₂ b →
    HasTerm (t₁ → t₂) (fun _ ↦ b)
  | fun_comp {α β γ : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} {t₃ : ProofType γ} {f : α → β}
    {g : β → γ} : HasTerm (t₁ → t₂) f → HasTerm (t₂ → t₃) g → HasTerm (t₁ → t₃) (g ∘ f)
  | fun_app {α β γ : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} {t₃ : ProofType γ}
    {f : α → β → γ} {g : α → β} : HasTerm (t₁ → t₂ → t₃) f → HasTerm (t₁ → t₂) g →
    HasTerm (t₁ → t₃) (fun a ↦ f a (g a))
  | fun_curry {α β γ : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} {t₃ : ProofType γ}
    {f : α × β → γ} (h : HasTerm (t₁ × t₂ → t₃) f) : HasTerm (t₁ → t₂ → t₃) (fun a b ↦ f (a, b))
  | unit : HasTerm unit ()
  | empty_elim {α : Type} {t : ProofType α} : HasTerm (empty → t) Empty.elim
  | prod_mk {α β : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} (a : α) (b : β) : HasTerm t₁ a →
    HasTerm t₂ b → HasTerm (t₁ × t₂) (a, b)
  | prod_fst {α β : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} : HasTerm (t₁ × t₂ → t₁) Prod.fst
  | prod_snd {α β : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} : HasTerm (t₁ × t₂ → t₂) Prod.snd
  | sum_inl  {α β : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} : HasTerm (t₁ → t₁ ⊕ t₂) Sum.inl
  | sum_inr  {α β : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} : HasTerm (t₂ → t₁ ⊕ t₂) Sum.inr
  | sum_elim {α β γ : Type} {t₁ : ProofType α} {t₂ : ProofType β} {t₃ : ProofType γ} {f : α → γ}
    {g : β → γ} : HasTerm (t₁ → t₃) f → HasTerm (t₂ → t₃) g → HasTerm (t₁ ⊕ t₂ → t₃) (Sum.elim f g)

end

namespace HasTerm

open Sequent

set_option pp.proofs true in
def toSequent {α : Type} {t : ProofType α} {a : α} (h : HasTerm t a) : ⊢ t.toWff :=
  match h with
  | @fun_abs β γ t₁ t₂ f abs => impII sorry
  | @fun_id β t => impII id
  | @fun_simpl β γ t₁ t₂ c h => impI (simpl h.toSequent)
  | @fun_syl β γ δ t₁ _t₂ t₃ f g h₁ h₂ =>
    impII (syl (impII_inv h₁.toSequent) (impII_inv h₂.toSequent))
  | @prod_mk β γ t₁ t₂ b c h₁ h₂ => andI h₁.toSequent h₂.toSequent
  | @sum_inl β γ t₁ t₂ b c h => orILD h.toSequent
  | @sum_inr β γ t₁ t₂ b c h => orIRD h.toSequent
  | @sum_elim β γ δ t₁ t₂ t₃ f g h₁ h₂ =>
    impII (orEI (impII_inv h₁.toSequent) (impII_inv h₂.toSequent))
  | @fun_curry β γ δ t₁ t₂ t₃ f h  => impII (impI (impII_inv h.toSequent))
  | @fun_app _β γ _t₁ t₂ f b h₁ h₂ => impE h₁.toSequent h₂.toSequent

end HasTerm

You can try something like this, which lets you create actual Lean proofs and prove that the proofs are "simple"

inductive IsSimpleProof : {α : Prop} → α → Prop
  | trivial : IsSimpleProof trivial
  | andIntro : IsSimpleProof And.intro
  | andLeft : IsSimpleProof And.left
  | andRight : IsSimpleProof And.right
  | orElim : IsSimpleProof Or.elim
  | orInl : IsSimpleProof Or.inl
  | orInr : IsSimpleProof Or.inr
  | app {a b : Prop} {f : a → b} {x : a} (hf : IsSimpleProof f) (hx : IsSimpleProof x) : IsSimpleProof (f x)

example : IsSimpleProof (α := True ∧ True) ⟨trivial, trivial⟩ :=
  .app (.app .andIntro .trivial) .trivial

It's cool, but at that point I don't see a reason to use Lean's proof terms, since we're constructing two proofs for everything instead of just using an inductive and forgetting about Lean proofs (i.e. we should drop the 2nd arg of IsSimpleProof, unless you really want Lean proof terms for some reason).

I've made something similar to IsSimpleProof:

set_option autoImplicit true

inductive IsPropFormula : Wff → Type where
  | trueInt : IsPropFormula ⊤
  | ident   : IsPropFormula (p → p)
  | const   : IsPropFormula p → IsPropFormula (q → p)
  | comp    : IsPropFormula (p → q) → IsPropFormula (q → r) → IsPropFormula (p → r)
  | falElim : IsPropFormula (⊥ → p)
  | andInt  : IsPropFormula (p → q) → IsPropFormula (p → r) → IsPropFormula (p → q ∧ r)
  | andFst  : IsPropFormula (p ∧ q → p)
  | andSnd  : IsPropFormula (p ∧ q → q)
  | orInl   : IsPropFormula (p → p ∨ q)
  | orInr   : IsPropFormula (p → q ∨ p)
  | orElim  : IsPropFormula (p → q ∨ r) → IsPropFormula (p ∧ q → s) → IsPropFormula (p ∧ r → s) →
    IsPropFormula (p → s)
  | curry   : IsPropFormula (p ∧ q → r) → IsPropFormula (p → (q → r))
  | app     : IsPropFormula (p → q) → IsPropFormula p → IsPropFormula q
  | frege   : IsPropFormula (p → q → r) → IsPropFormula (p → q) → IsPropFormula (p → r)

The constructor IsPropFormula.mp is the modus ponens inference rule. I managed to use the constructors of the inductive type IsPropFormula to prove every axiom of a Hilbert system for constructive propositional logic.

namespace IsPropFormula

def ax01 {p : Wff} : IsPropFormula (p → p) :=
  ident

def ax02 {p q : Wff} : IsPropFormula (p → q → p) :=
  curry andFst

def ax03 {p q r : Wff} : IsPropFormula ((p → q → r) → ((p → q) → (p → r))) :=
  curry <| curry <|
    frege
      (frege (comp andFst andFst) andSnd)
      (frege (comp andFst andSnd) andSnd)

def ax04 {p : Wff} : IsPropFormula ((p → ¬p) → ¬p) :=
  curry (frege (frege andFst andSnd) andSnd)

def ax05 {p q : Wff} : IsPropFormula (¬p → p → q) :=
  curry (comp (frege andFst andSnd) falElim)

      (impII_inv h₃.toSequent))
  | @curry q r s h => impII (impI (impII_inv h.toSequent))
  | @app _q r h₁ h₂ => mp (impII_inv h₁.toSequent) h₂.toSequent
  | @frege q _r s h₁ h₂ => impII (impE (impII_inv h₁.toSequent) (impII_inv h₂.toSequent))

end IsPropFormula

namespace Sequent

open IsPropFormula

def isPropFormula {p q : Wff} (d : p ⊢ q) : IsPropFormula (p → q) :=
  match d with
  | .id => ident
  | @simpl r s d => const (app d.isPropFormula trueInt)
  | @syl φ _χ ψ d₁ d₂ => comp d₁.isPropFormula d₂.isPropFormula
  | falE => falElim
  | @andI φ χ θ d₁ d₂ => andInt d₁.isPropFormula d₂.isPropFormula
  | @andEL χ θ => andFst
  | @andER χ θ => andSnd
  | @orIL  χ θ => orInl
  | @orIR  χ θ => orInr
  | @orE φ _χ _θ ψ or left right => orElim or.isPropFormula left.isPropFormula right.isPropFormula
  | @impI χ θ ψ d => curry d.isPropFormula
  | @impE φ _χ ψ d₁ d₂ => frege d₁.isPropFormula d₂.isPropFormula

end Sequent

theorem not_em_propvar {p : PropVar} (hp : ⊢ .fromVar p ∨ ¬.fromVar p) : False := by
  let it3 : Wff PropVar → Fin 3 :=
    Wff.rec
      (fromVar := fun _ => 1)
      (Tru := 2) (Fal := 0)
      (And := fun _ _ a b =>
        ⟨min a.1 b.1, Nat.lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.min_le_left a.1 b.1) a.2⟩)
      (Or := fun _ _ a b =>
        ⟨max a.1 b.1, Nat.max_lt.2 ⟨a.2, b.2⟩⟩)
      (Imp := fun _ _ a b =>
        if a ≤ b then 2 else b)
  have hi3 {φ ψ} : it3 (φ → ψ) = 2 ↔ it3 φ ≤ it3 ψ := by
    constructor
    · intro h
      apply @Decidable.byContradiction _ (Fin.decLe _ _)
      intro hn
      apply hn
      exact le_of_le_of_eq (Fin.le_last _) (h.symm.trans (if_neg hn))
    · intro h
      exact if_pos h
  suffices h : ∀ φ, (⊢ φ) → it3 φ = 2 from
    of_decide_eq_false rfl (h _ hp)
  intro φ hφ
  induction hφ with
  | ident => exact if_pos (Fin.le_refl _)
  | simpl _ ih =>
    apply hi3.mpr
    exact le_of_le_of_eq (Fin.le_last _) ih.symm
  | syl _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    exact hi3.mpr (Fin.le_trans (hi3.mp ih₁) (hi3.mp ih₂))
  | mp _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    apply Fin.le_antisymm (Fin.le_last _)
    exact le_of_eq_of_le ih₂.symm (hi3.mp ih₁)
  | truI => rfl
  | falE => exact (@hi3 ⊥ _).mpr (Fin.zero_le _)
  | andID _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    apply (@hi3 _ (_ ∧ _)).mpr
    exact Nat.le_min_of_le_of_le (hi3.mp ih₁) (hi3.mp ih₂)
  | andEL =>
    apply (@hi3 (_ ∧ _) _).mpr
    exact Nat.min_le_left _ _
  | andER =>
    apply (@hi3 (_ ∧ _) _).mpr
    exact Nat.min_le_right _ _
  | orIL =>
    apply (@hi3 _ (_ ∨ _)).mpr
    exact Nat.le_max_left _ _
  | orIR =>
    apply (@hi3 _ (_ ∨ _)).mpr
    exact Nat.le_max_right _ _
  | orED _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
    apply hi3.mpr
    apply @Fin.le_trans _ _ (it3 (_ ∧ (_ ∨ _))) _ (Nat.le_min_of_le_of_le
      (Nat.le_refl (it3 _).1) ((@hi3 _ (_ ∨ _)).mp ih₁))
    apply @Fin.le_trans _ _ (it3 ((_ ∧ _) ∨ (_ ∧ _))) _
      (Nat.le_of_eq (Nat.min_max_distrib_left _ _ _))
    exact Nat.max_le_of_le_of_le ((@hi3 (_ ∧ _) _).mp ih₂) ((@hi3 (_ ∧ _) _).mp ih₃)
  | @impI φ ψ _ _ ih =>
    apply (@hi3 _ (_ → _)).mpr
    refine (Fin.le_total (it3 φ) (it3 ψ)).elim
      (fun h => ?_) (fun h => ?_)
    · apply @Fin.le_trans _ _ (it3 (_ ∧ _)) _
        (Nat.le_of_eq (Nat.min_eq_left h).symm)
      apply Fin.le_trans ((@hi3 (_ ∧ _) _).mp ih)
      exact iteInduction (motive := fun u => it3 _ ≤ u)
        (fun _ => Fin.le_last _) (fun _ => Fin.le_refl _)
    · refine le_of_le_of_eq (Fin.le_last _) (hi3.mpr ?_).symm
      refine Fin.le_trans ?_ ((@hi3 (_ ∧ _) _).mp ih)
      exact Nat.le_of_eq (Nat.min_eq_right h).symm
  | @impED _ ψ χ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
    apply hi3.mpr
    refine @Decidable.byCases (it3 ψ ≤ it3 χ) _ (Fin.decLe _ _)
      (fun h => ?_) (fun h => ?_)
    · exact Fin.le_trans (hi3.mp ih₂) h
    · apply le_of_le_of_eq ((@hi3 _ (_ → _)).mp ih₁)
      exact if_neg h
